\section*{Appendix D — Evaluation detail}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix D — Evaluation detail}

\subsection*{D.1 Ablations}
\noindent Each row is a full re-run measured against the anchor
sets. Recall is reported at the depth where the change was decided.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{2.2cm}p{4.6cm}p{2.3cm}p{6.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
\hd{Stage} & \hd{Change} & \hd{Recall} & \hd{Diagnosis} \\
\midrule
Router & clause text alone & 54.8\% @3 & short clauses carry almost no signal \\
Router & + structural context & \textbf{90.5\% @3} & a clause is scoped by its heading and stem \\
Router & + dense embeddings & 92.5\% @3 & fixes vocabulary mismatch (HR $\to$ Personnel Security, 0/8 $\to$ 8/8) \\
Candidates & baseline & 69.2\% @10 & enhancements crowd out base controls \\
Candidates & + base quota, parent lift & \textbf{92.3\% @10} & SAMA is principle-level; the base control is the right target \\
Candidates & + assessment text removed & 76.9\% @10 & a correction, not a regression --- see D.2 \\
Candidates & + control discussion text & 84.6\% @10 & widens vocabulary against domain synonymy \\
Candidates & + retrieval-specific query & \textbf{92.3\% @3} & routing and retrieval need different queries \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}

\subsection*{D.2 Assessment-procedure contamination}
\noindent The public OSCAL release merges SP 800-53 controls with
SP 800-53A \emph{assessment procedures} in one file. A naive parse pulls lists
of documents to examine and roles to interview into the control statement,
inflating it by up to 84\%. That noise raised apparent recall from 76.9\% to
92.3\% through accidental matching: the extra vocabulary matched clauses the
control itself does not address. Cleaning the source lowered the headline
number and made it honest. A metric that improves after data cleaning deserves
suspicion; one that falls deserves trust.

\subsection*{D.3 Risk--coverage}
\noindent Computed on the single-judge findings, before the
debate layer; the debated run accepts 335 judgments at the same threshold,
because arbiter rulings resolve cases the proposer left under-confident.
Confidence is not continuous: it clusters, so the threshold selects a band
rather than a point.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrr@{}}\toprule
\hd{$\tau$} & \hd{Accepted judgments} & \hd{Coverage} \\
\midrule
0.40 & 491 & 93\% \\
0.50 & 377 & 71\% \\
0.55 & 318 & 60\% \\
\textbf{0.60} & \textbf{186} & \textbf{35\%} \\
0.65 & 146 & 27\% \\
0.70 & 113 & 21\% \\
0.80 & 46 & 8\% \\
\bottomrule\end{tabular}\end{center}

\subsection*{D.4 Band accuracy, and why not calibration}
\noindent Human review of the stratified sample, split by the band
the system assigned:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.6cm}rr@{}}\toprule
\hd{Band} & \hd{Range} & \hd{Correct} & \hd{Precision} \\
\midrule
high confidence & $\geq 0.70$ & 13/14 & 92.9\% \\
medium confidence & 0.60--0.70 & 14/16 & 87.5\% \\
\bottomrule\end{tabular}\end{center}
\noindent The ordering holds --- the higher band is the more
accurate --- but both bands exceed the accuracy their own bounds imply. The
system is \emph{ordered}, not \emph{calibrated}: a 0.75 score does not mean a
75\% chance of being right, it means a better chance than a 0.60 score. This is
why the report says \emph{banded confidence} and reports no expected
calibration error.
